title: What the data says about immigrants in the U.S.
summary: Pew Research Center analysis shows the U.S. immigrant population peaked at 53.3 million in January 2025 and fell to about 51.9 million by June 2025 amid policy changes, higher deportations, and fewer arrivals. The U.S. still hosts the largest immigrant population globally. In 2023 there were record highs in unauthorized immigrants (14 million). Origins, legal status, labor-force participation, English proficiency and geographic concentrations are examined, and shifts in origin regions since 2015 are highlighted.
content:
Numbers, Facts and Trends Shaping Your World

After more than 50 years of rapid growth, the nation’s immigrant population is now in decline.

In January 2025, 53.3 million immigrants lived in the United States – the largest number ever recorded. In the ensuing months, however, more immigrants left the country or were deported than arrived. By June, the country’s foreign-born population had shrunk by more than a million people, marking its first decline since the 1960s.

A new Pew Research Center analysis of Census Bureau data finds that, as of June 2025, 51.9 million immigrants lived in the U.S., making up 15.4% of the nation’s population. This was down from January, when there were a record 53.3 million immigrants in the U.S., accounting for 15.8% of the country’s population – the highest percentage on record.

Starting in mid-2024, several policy changes have affected the U.S. immigrant population. Policy shifts and enforcement changes likely contributed to the decline in the unauthorized immigrant population between January and June 2025: border crossings fell to lows not seen since the 1960s, immigration arrests and deportations increased, and a growing number of immigrants lost deportation protections or chose to leave the country.

Pew Research Center conducted this analysis to answer common questions about immigration to the United States and the U.S. immigrant population. The immigrant or foreign-born population consists of people born outside of the United States or its territories who are not U.S. citizens at birth. Estimates for 2025 are from Pew Research Center tabulations of the Census Bureau’s monthly Current Population Surveys, accessed through IPUMS. The Current Population Survey’s June 2025 estimate was the most recent available as of July 31. Note that the recent downward trend in the estimated U.S. immigrant population may in part be due to technical reasons such as declining CPS survey participation among immigrants.

Data on characteristics and legal status of U.S. immigrants in 2023 comes from Center analysis of augmented and supplemented 2023 American Community Survey data (IPUMS). The analysis also includes historical data from decennial censuses. The 2023 ACS was supplemented to take into account the Census Bureau’s 2024 revisions to their population estimates based on increased levels of net international migration.

Comparative data on other countries around the world comes from the United Nations’ migrant stock and overall population estimates for 2024. Even as the nation’s immigrant population has declined in recent months—a change that may be partly artificial due to a declining survey response rate among immigrants—the U.S. is home to more immigrants than any other country. As of 2024, the second-largest immigrant population is in Germany, numbering around 17 million, according to the United Nations.

While the U.S. is home to the largest number of immigrants, dozens of countries have a higher proportion of immigrants in their populations than the U.S. does. In neighboring Canada, for example, immigrants account for 22% of the population. And in the United Arab Emirates, about three-quarters of all residents were born elsewhere.

As of mid-2023, more than 11 million U.S. residents were born in Mexico, representing 22% of all immigrants nationally. The second-largest immigrant group was from India (3.2 million, or 6%), followed by China (3 million, or 6%), the Philippines (2.1 million, or 4%) and Cuba (1.7 million, or 3%). About half of all U.S. immigrants (52%, or 26.7 million people) were born in Latin America. In addition to migrants from Mexico and Cuba, more than a million hail from El Salvador (1.6 million), Guatemala (1.4 million), the Dominican Republic (1.4 million), Colombia (1.2 million), Honduras (1.1 million) and Venezuela (1.1 million).

After Latin America, Asia is the second-largest region of birth for U.S. immigrants. In 2023, around a quarter of all immigrants (27%, or nearly 14 million people) were born in Asia. About 11 million immigrants came from every other world region combined, accounting for 22% of the U.S. foreign-born population: 10% were born in Europe, 5% in sub-Saharan Africa, 4% in the Middle East-North Africa region, and 2% in Canada or another North American country.

An unprecedented number of immigrants—more than 11 million—arrived in the U.S. between 2020 and 2025. That included more than 3 million in 2023 alone, the largest annual total ever recorded, according to Center analysis of government data sources. Alongside this increase, immigrants’ origin regions have shifted, with a growing share coming from South America and Europe and a declining share coming from Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Between 2021 and 2023, 20% of newly arrived immigrants were from South America, up from 13% in 2015-19; 12% were from Europe or Canada, up from 9% in the earlier period. Conversely, 24% of new arrivals between 2021 and 2023 were from South and East Asia, down from 29% in 2015-19, and 5% were from sub-Saharan Africa, down from 8%.

Mexico was the largest origin country for immigrants who arrived between 2021 and 2023, accounting for about 11% of arrivals in that period. Other top origin countries for recent arrivals included India (8%), Venezuela (7%), Cuba (6%) and Colombia (5%). Throughout this period, unauthorized immigrants accounted for most new immigrant arrivals, with many coming from Central and South America.

Since 1965, more than 76 million immigrants have come to the U.S. The 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act opened immigration pathways from Asia and Latin America, changing the composition and scale of immigration flows. The Immigration Act of 1990 further increased legal immigration and broadened the countries of origin. Today, Mexico remains the largest origin country among U.S. immigrants, although immigration from Mexico has slowed since 2007 and the Mexican-born population in the U.S. has declined; the Mexican share of the U.S. immigrant population fell from 29% in 2010 to 22% in 2023.

As of 2023, 46% of immigrants were naturalized U.S. citizens. Nearly a quarter (23%) were lawful permanent residents ("green card holders"), and another 4% were lawful temporary residents permitted to stay for limited periods, typically for work or study. The remaining immigrants fell into the "unauthorized" category and constituted 27% of all U.S. immigrants.

Unauthorized immigrants are those without full legal status. As of 2023, this population hit a new record high of 14 million. Within this group, about 6 million (a little more than 40%) had some form of temporary protection from deportation, with some also having a permit to work in the U.S. Among those with protections were 2.6 million asylum applicants; 700,000 people who entered legally after receiving parole; 700,000 victims of crime and violence; 650,000 people with Temporary Protected Status (TPS); and 600,000 immigrants who were brought to the U.S. as children and are enrolled in the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program.

Another 1 million migrants encountered U.S. Border Patrol before being released into the U.S., typically with an order to appear in immigration court. These immigrants have had more limited protections from deportation while their cases are resolved. Immigrants in these groups are included as part of the "unauthorized" population because their deportation protections are temporary and can change quickly. The Trump administration rescinded deportation protections and work permits for about 500,000 immigrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua and Venezuela who entered the U.S. legally. The remaining unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. as of 2023 (about 8 million) had neither legal status nor temporary protection from deportation.

Immigrants who are lawful permanent residents and meet other requirements can apply to become U.S. citizens through naturalization. During fiscal 2024, 818,500 immigrants became U.S. citizens through naturalization. Millions of lawful permanent residents are currently eligible to naturalize but have not applied.

Labor force data for 2023 show 33 million immigrants were in the U.S. workforce, including about 23 million lawful immigrants and 10 million unauthorized immigrants. Immigrants comprised nearly one-in-five workers (19%) in 2023, up from 15% two decades earlier and 12% in 1995. About 2% of adult immigrants, including noncitizens, are currently serving in the military or served in the past.

Geographic concentration is notable: in 2023, most of the nation’s 51.8 million immigrants lived in just four states. California had 11.3 million immigrants (28.4% of the national total), followed by Texas (over 6 million), Florida (5.4 million) and New York (5.0 million). A majority of immigrants lived in 12 metropolitan areas; the New York City metro area held 13% of all immigrants, Los Angeles 9%, and Miami 6%.

Overall, immigrants in the U.S. had lower levels of educational attainment than their U.S.-born counterparts in 2023, although attainment varies widely by region of origin. English proficiency among immigrants ages 5 and older stood at 52% (those who speak English very well or only English at home), with higher proficiency for immigrants who arrived earlier. For example, 57% of immigrants who arrived before 2000 are proficient English speakers, compared with 47% who arrived in 2010 or later.

Note: This analysis updates an earlier Pew Research Center piece originally published May 3, 2017. The report and tabulations draw on multiple data sources, including the Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey and American Community Survey, supplemented with Center adjustments and United Nations comparative estimates.

About the authors: Stephanie Kramer is a senior researcher at Pew Research Center. Jeffrey S. Passel is a senior demographer at Pew Research Center.
